sections.b: The book opens with the only part written in Greek from the start: the grandson's foreword. It names Israel's books three times in three groups (the law, the prophets, and "the others"), an early witness to the three-part Jewish Bible. It dates his arrival in Egypt to "the thirty-eighth year under King Euergetes": 132 BC, counting the years of the second king of that name from 170 BC. And it contains a translator's apology: "Words spoken in Hebrew do not carry the same force when they are carried over into another language."

sections.h: Ben Sira: Wisdom created first, given through the commandments
sections.b: Sirach opens, "All wisdom comes from the Lord" (Sirach 1:1). Like Proverbs 8, it says Wisdom "was created first of all things" (Sirach 1:4) and was poured out on all God's works, but given freely to those who love him. Ben Sira's own step is to bind Wisdom to the law: "If you have set your heart on wisdom, guard the commandments, / and the Lord will provide her for you" (Sirach 1:26). In Sirach 4:11–19 Wisdom is a mother and teacher who tests her pupils by hard ways before she trusts them; in the Hebrew she speaks in her own voice. In Sirach 6:18–37 she is a field to plow and a yoke to wear, whose fetters become a shelter and whose collar a robe of glory, a picture that Matthew 11:28–30 recalls.
sections.refs: Sirach 1:1–10; Sirach 1:26; Sirach 4:11–19; Sirach 6:18–37; Proverbs 8:22–31; Matthew 11:28–30

common: Ben Sira identifies Wisdom with the law of Moses (Sirach 24:23), and his chapter 1 already ties her to keeping the commandments.

sections.h: Ben Sira's hymn to the fear of the Lord
sections.b: No book praises the fear of the Lord more than Sirach. Its first chapter is a hymn to it: "The fear of the Lord is glory and pride, / gladness and a garland of joy" (Sirach 1:11). It is the start, the fullness, the crown and the root of wisdom (Sirach 1:14, 16, 18, 20). Chapter 2 repeats "you who fear the Lord" and "those who fear the Lord" as refrains (Sirach 2:7–9, 15–17): those who fear him wait for his mercy, keep his ways, and are filled with the law. Even friendship rests on it: "those who fear the Lord will find" a faithful friend (Sirach 6:16).
sections.refs: Sirach 1:11–20; Sirach 1:27–30; Sirach 2:7–17; Sirach 6:16–17; Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 9:10

sections.b: Ben Sira says, "A blazing fire is put out by water, / and sins are atoned for by alms" (Sirach 3:30). The Hebrew of the Cairo manuscript has tsedaqah, "righteousness," with the temple verb kipper; the grandson's Greek eleēmosynē shows he took it as giving to the poor. The same word is used for kindness to an aging father, which "in place of your sins ... will be built up for you" (Sirach 3:14). Chapter 4 adds the practice: do not keep the poor waiting, do not turn your face from them, and do not keep your hand "stretched out for taking / and pulled in tight when it comes to paying back" (Sirach 4:31), a saying the Didache closely echoes. Churches differ over whether such giving takes away sin; see the card at Tobit 4.
sections.refs: Sirach 3:14; Sirach 3:30; Sirach 4:1–10; Sirach 4:31; Tobit 4:10; Tobit 12:9; Daniel 4:27; Didache 4:5–6

sections.h: Ben Sira's sermon on the fifth commandment
sections.b: Sirach 3:1–16 is a long sermon on "Honor your father and your mother" (Exodus 20:12). Ben Sira keeps the promise of long life (Sirach 3:6) and adds more: the one who honors a father "makes atonement for sins" and is heard in prayer (Sirach 3:3, 5). He speaks to grown sons: "support your father in his old age" and be patient "if his understanding fades" (Sirach 3:12–13). The Catholic Catechism quotes this passage on the duties of adult children (2218).
sections.refs: Sirach 3:1–16; Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16; Exodus 21:17; Ephesians 6:1–3; Mark 7:10–13

sections.b: Ben Sira taught young men who would have money and power, and he bound them to the poor: "do not rob the poor man of what he lives on, / and do not drag out the wait for eyes that look to you in need" (Sirach 4:1). The poor man's bitter cry reaches "the one who made him" (Sirach 4:6). The one who is a father to orphans and a husband to their mother "will be as a son of the Most High" (Sirach 4:10), words Jesus uses in Luke 6:35. In the Hebrew of 4:10 the reward is that God will call him son and rescue him from the Pit.
sections.refs: Sirach 4:1–10; Deuteronomy 24:14–15; Exodus 22:22–24; Proverbs 14:31; Luke 6:35; James 1:27; James 5:4

sections.b: Speech is one of Ben Sira's favorite subjects. "Be swift when it comes to listening, / and give your reply with patience" (Sirach 5:11) stands close to James 1:19. "Talk can bring glory, and it can bring disgrace, / and a man's own tongue is what makes him fall" (Sirach 5:13). He warns against the man with "two tongues," who winnows in every wind (Sirach 5:9; 6:1), and against the gossip (Sirach 5:14), and he praises speech that is single and steady: "let what you say be one thing" (Sirach 5:10; compare Matthew 5:37).
sections.refs: Sirach 1:29; Sirach 4:23–29; Sirach 5:9–6:1; Sirach 6:5; James 1:19; James 3:2–10; Matthew 5:37

sections.h: Ben Sira: do not lean on riches
sections.b: "Do not rest your weight on your possessions, / and do not say, 'It is enough for me'" (Sirach 5:1). Ben Sira warns that money "gotten by wrong" will do no good "on the day disaster strikes" (Sirach 5:8); the Hebrew calls it "false riches." His humility is meant for the rich in particular: the Hebrew of 3:17 reads "when you are rich, walk humbly." Compare Jesus' rich fool (Luke 12:15–21) and "the wealth of dishonesty" (Luke 16:9).
sections.refs: Sirach 3:17; Sirach 5:1–8; Proverbs 11:28; Psalm 49:6; Luke 12:15–21; Luke 16:9

sections.h: The prologue to Sirach: law, prophets and "the others"
sections.b: Writing in Egypt after 132 BC, Ben Sira's grandson names Israel's books three times: "the law and the prophets and the others who came after them," "the law, the prophets and the other books of our ancestors," and "the law itself, the prophecies and the rest of the books" (Sirach 1:0). It is an early witness to the three-part Jewish Bible. It shows a recognized third group but does not name it or list its books, so readers differ on whether it was already closed. Compare "the Law of Moses ... the Prophets and ... the Psalms" (Luke 24:44).

sections.h: The grandson's apology for his translation
sections.b: The prologue to Sirach is an early comment on translating Scripture, written about 132 BC: "Words spoken in Hebrew do not carry the same force when they are carried over into another language," and even the law, the prophecies and the other books "have no small difference when read in their own tongue" (Sirach 1:0). It shows that Greek translations of the law and the prophets already existed. Where the Hebrew of Ben Sira survives, it often differs from the Greek: the Hebrew of manuscript A has a root and a planting where the Greek has houses (Sirach 3:9), and "discipline" where the Greek has "wisdom" (Sirach 6:22). Manuscript A is a medieval copy, so some differences may be the grandson's and some may be later changes in the Hebrew; which way a difference went cannot always be known.

sections.h: "Do not hold off from turning to the Lord"
sections.b: Ben Sira warns against presuming on mercy: "Do not say, 'I sinned, and what did it do to me?' / For the Lord is long-suffering" (Sirach 5:4), and "Do not hold off from turning to the Lord, / and do not push it from one day to the next" (Sirach 5:7). The Hebrew has shuv, "turn," the Bible's word for repentance; the Latin, "Delay not to be converted to the Lord," became a classic call to conversion. He also teaches not to be ashamed of "confessing your sins" (Sirach 4:26), where the Hebrew says "turning back from sin."
sections.refs: Sirach 4:26; Sirach 5:4–7; Romans 2:4; Hebrews 3:13; 2 Corinthians 6:2; Proverbs 28:13

sections.h: Ben Sira: serving God means being tested
sections.b: "My child, if you step forward to be a servant of the Lord God, / make your soul ready for testing" (Sirach 2:1). Ben Sira treats hardship as testing, not abandonment: "Fire is where gold is proved" (Sirach 2:5), and history shows that no one who trusted the Lord was left alone (Sirach 2:10). Wisdom, too, tests her pupils with fear and torment before she trusts them (Sirach 4:17). James 1:2–4 and 1 Peter 1:6–7 teach much the same.

sections.h: Ben Sira: mercy as great as God himself
sections.b: "The Lord is full of pity and mercy; / he forgives sins and rescues in the hour of distress" (Sirach 2:11), an echo of Exodus 34:6. "For as his greatness is, / so too is his mercy" (Sirach 2:18). But mercy is no license: "mercy and anger are both with him, / and his fury settles down on sinners" (Sirach 5:6).
sections.refs: Sirach 2:7–11; Sirach 2:18; Sirach 5:4–7; Exodus 34:6–7; James 5:11; Romans 11:22

sections.h: Ben Sira: wisdom through the law
sections.b: Ben Sira joins wisdom to the law of Moses: "If you have set your heart on wisdom, guard the commandments" (Sirach 1:26); those who love God "will be filled full of the law" (Sirach 2:16); and the way to wisdom is to "murmur over his commandments at all times" (Sirach 6:37). The grandson's prologue says the book was written so that readers "grow much further in a life lived by the law" (Sirach 1:0).
sections.refs: Sirach 1:0; Sirach 1:26; Sirach 2:15–16; Sirach 6:37; Psalm 1:2; Deuteronomy 4:6

sections.h: "Do not dig into things stronger than you are"
sections.b: Ben Sira warns against prying into what is hidden: "Do not go looking for things harder than you can handle, / and do not dig into things stronger than you are. / Turn your mind to what you have been told to do; / the hidden things are nothing you need" (Sirach 3:21–22). The Babylonian Talmud quotes these lines in Hebrew by name from "the book of Ben Sira" (Hagigah 13a) in setting limits on speculation about divine mysteries.

sections.h: Ben Sira on testing and keeping friends
sections.b: Sirach 6:5–17 is a long passage on friendship. Kind speech wins friends, but "When you get a friend, get him by putting him to the test" (Sirach 6:7). Three kinds of false friend follow: the one who is a friend "only in his own season," the one who turns to hatred, and the one "who shares your table" but vanishes in trouble (Sirach 6:8–10). Then the praise: "A faithful friend is a solid roof over you, / and the man who has found him has found treasure" (Sirach 6:14); he is "a medicine that gives life" (Sirach 6:16; the Hebrew has "a bundle of life"), and "those who fear the Lord will find him." The Talmud quotes Sirach 6:6: "reveal your secrets to one in a thousand" (Sanhedrin 100b).

In Sirach 6:30 the Hebrew of the Cairo manuscript A calls Wisdom's ropes petil tekhelet, "a cord of blue," the very words of the law of tassels (Numbers 15:38); the Qumran fragment 2Q18 keeps only the last letters of the line. Read this way, Wisdom's bonds look like the commandments every Israelite wore at the corners of his clothes.

sections.h: Rest at the end of Wisdom's yoke
sections.b: Ben Sira promises the one who takes Wisdom's fetters and collar: "When it is all over, you will come upon her rest" (Sirach 6:28). Jesus' invitation has the same shape: "Lift my yoke onto yourselves and learn from me ... And you will find rest for your souls" (Matthew 11:29).
